comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Decided: portable core in Rust, native per-OS shell, one C ABI symbol carrying protobuf between them. Full case, alternatives and consequences in docs/mip/0001-portable-core.md (MIP-1).

What stage 1 taught, which is what this card was waiting for:

1. The core stayed OS-free without discipline. 1269 lines, four files importing anything at all. So the portability risk Swift was meant to carry never showed up as a code problem - which means moving it is a port, not an unpicking.
2. Both dependencies are C APIs. libghostty's surface embedding is NSView-shaped and stays in the shell whatever happens; libghostty-vt is language-neutral, and herdr already drives its key encoder from Rust.
3. The decisive one, which is not about Swift's quality: a Linux or Windows shell will not be Swift either, because Swift's GUI story off Apple is not something to bet on. So a Swift core does not avoid the FFI boundary - it relocates it to Rust-calling-Swift, the direction that needs hand-written @_cdecl exports, manual ownership, and the Swift runtime shipped inside a Rust binary, on the platform where we would have the least tooling to debug it.

Timing: the core is the smallest it will ever be and the plan was about to triple it with the mirror. Porting now is days; porting after Stage 2 is a rewrite of the spine.

creator: Alexander Terp
description: All-Swift with a headless Swift package, or a portable core (Rust/Go) from day one? Current lean (docs/origin.md): Swift-first, portability enforced by contract tests and shared corpora. Decide after stage 1 teaches us the real shape.
title: Decide the shell/core language split
